name: Lighting / smiling side meta

lead: This meta covers choosing which side of the face to show, using lighting that flatters it, and practising an even smile.
It is discussed as a way to look more symmetrical in photos. Published research looks at smile symmetry in clinical settings but has not tested these tactics.

paras: Practitioners aim to change how light and shadow fall on the face and to equalise how far each mouth corner lifts. Whether training changes smile symmetry has not been studied.
No documented harms are reported for the practice itself. Facial paralysis surgery, a separate topic, carries procedure-specific risks.

lead: The lighting and smiling side meta is a set of photo-and-presentation tactics in looksmaxxing circles concerned with which side of the face is shown to a camera, how the light falls on it, and how evenly a person smiles. The stated aim is to make a face look more symmetrical or more attractive in photographs and in person by working around uneven smiles and lopsided features.

The sources available for this entry are thin. No published study has tested the practice as described by its followers, namely choosing a flattering side, adjusting lighting, or training the smile for evenness. Related clinical literature exists on smile symmetry in general dental populations [1][2] and on surgical rehabilitation of smiles in people with facial paralysis [3][4], but these concern different questions.
infobox: More even-looking smile and flattering photographic presentation
No direct studies of the practice
Smile symmetry in dentistry; facial reanimation surgery

paras: Proponents describe the meta as having two linked parts. The first is choosing a preferred side of the face to present, and arranging lighting so that shadows and highlights favour it. The second is smile training: practising in a mirror so that both mouth corners rise by a similar amount, or so that a smile looks less lopsided.

Dental researchers have studied how common smile asymmetry is and how smile features relate to perceived attractiveness. A study of an adult population in southern Europe examined the prevalence of alterations in smile symmetry characteristics [2], and a 2022 paper reviewed morphological features of smile attractiveness and their relation to perception and gingival aesthetic parameters [1]. These studies concern clinical measurement and perception rather than self-directed training.

A separate surgical literature addresses smile restoration in patients with facial nerve palsy, including free muscle transfer [3][4] and procedures that weaken the depressor anguli oris muscle to improve symmetry in post-paralysis palsy [5]. These treat a medical condition and are not studies of cosmetic smile practice.

No studies found. Studies of smile symmetry in dental populations [2] and of surgical smile rehabilitation in facial palsy [3][4][5] exist, but none tests lighting choices, side selection or smile training for cosmetic evenness.
